items.title: Hear the Guard First: your exchange in one piece
items.my_version:
Whichever protective part showed up, try talking to it in the same Nurturer voice you meant for your little one. At some point you can ask that part, "What are you afraid would happen if you stepped back?"

It might say this will just be one more performance, and you'll fool yourself again. That one can sting, because there could be something to it. Maybe you've fooled yourself before, and that part remembers. "Tell me what you remember, I'm listening." works well here. It puts you into the role of the Nurturer, which alleviates the instinct to argue back. Usually your little one only comes forward after that part feels heard. Peek-a-boo! If you push past it, you might get exactly the performance it was afraid of. Even if you didn't win an Emmy last year, that can look convincing, with the right words and maybe even tears, while nothing underneath feels any safer.

A harder voice can seem more fitting for something that's been in your way. I'd still keep the Nurturer voice. If that voice isn't there in you yet, borrow it from someone who's been safe for you.

A new roommate doesn't win you over with a speech on move-in day (hopefully, right?). The rent just has to keep showing up. Your Protector earns that guard's trust about the same way, mostly out in ordinary life. The things you do can be small, like keeping a promise to yourself nobody else knew about. Or saying no to someone, and not texting an hour later to take it back. That second one can be really hard.

That part doesn't have to move out. It's been living there way longer than the grown-up you. It can keep watch while you take one small step toward your little one. I think watching is what it wants anyway, to find out if there's a grown-up here now who could call it all off if things got to be too much. It doesn't have to be all or nothing, either. Maybe it would settle for a lighter cover for now, like blinds tilted open a crack, and let you peek out for a minute (ST-CA, section 9.3.4). If it says no, I'd listen. When it lets you, keep an eye on that part too, for any change at all.

If it's been calling all this stupid, it might turn out to be scared of getting its hopes up. I wouldn't want to get mine up either. I'd tell it something like, "You don't have to hope yet, I'll keep coming back even when I mess up." Sometimes it doesn't say anything back for a while.

Blaming yourself can be doing a protective job, too. "It's all my fault" might be your parent's line, word for word. Then again, if it's your fault, maybe you can fix it before they leave. I'd stop the cruelty either way. And I'd get curious about what makes it so hard to give up.

items.title: Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff: the danger lines back with the dream line
items.where: Before You Tell the Hardest Stuff, P1
items.your_version:
Then there’s the stuff that’s hardest to tell anyone, and of course that's exactly what you need help with. Maybe it’s an urge that scares you, or something you did that could get you in legal trouble. I'd assume that what you tell won't be completely confidential, especially if it sounds like something dangerous.

You know that DM you deleted? It can still be sitting on their phone as a screenshot 🙈, and whatever’s on a company’s server can get handed over if a court asks. Just because Mr. Boopaloopa was your name on WhatsApp doesn't guarantee you're anonymous, by the way.

And some of the people you’d tell, like therapists, teachers, and doctors, can be required to report certain things (a few laws cover everybody, too). Which things depends on where you live, and it’s nowhere near every crime you might mention. The cops are hopefully the obvious ones to be careful with, even if they pretend to care.

So I’d ask this person, before handing over any tricky specifics: “What does the law require you to report?” That's a normal and expected question. Although personally I wouldn't even bother with that, because whatever they tell you today, the law can change tomorrow.

You can always rephrase things as a dream narrative to get the emotional content across without triggering alarm bells (although I actually got in trouble with TalkSpace therapy bot even for a dream!). Just don’t hold back a danger that’s happening now from people who can help, and get anyone in danger safe before worrying about the rest. Sometimes telling on yourself is the thing that keeps someone safe, whatever it costs you legally.

items.title: Ill Will and Loving-Kindness: the line before the question
items.my_version: In one of the Buddha's own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it's hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it's not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you're the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you'd be the one burning. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?
items.before: In one of the Buddha's own accounts of how he woke up, ill will shows up in his mind and he sees it's hurting him. If he had to figure that out by watching, it's not obvious. Ill will can make you feel powerful. Being on fire would too, and people would definitely get out of your way, but unless you're the Human Torch from the Fantastic Four, you'd be the one burning. So it's worth noticing what it's doing to you. Has it ever left anybody at ease, with nothing to regret afterward?

items.title: Borrow Love: the life's-journey line
items.where: Borrow Love—or Borrow the Perspective of Care, P3
items.my_version: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, your bank account and all, and then step outside it and ask what you'd tell them. It's a cheap trick for becoming the outsider to your own mess. And the gap it gets around even has a name, Solomon's paradox, after the king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.
items.before: Or put somebody you care about into your exact life, your family, your bank account and all, and then step outside it and ask what you'd tell them. It's a cheap trick for becoming the outsider to your own mess. The quest for self-knowledge is a life's journey, but you don't have to wait for your life to finish to figure out your best next move. And the gap it gets around even has a name, Solomon's paradox, after the king everybody brought their disputes to, who then wrecked his own life.

items.title: Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust: the moral after Mr. Rogers
items.where: Love Doesn't Have to Wait for Trust ❤️, P8
items.my_version: You can see the same move in a dramatized scene from the movie A Beautiful Day in the Neighborhood. Lloyd, a reporter, tells Mr. Rogers, "I can't imagine it was easy… growing up with you as a father." He doesn't collapse under that or fight it, but he does answer what's worth answering in it. He tells Lloyd that until recently his oldest son never told people about his dad, and his youngest "genuinely tested" him. Eventually he and his youngest found their way, and now he's very proud of both his sons. Then he says, "But you are right, Lloyd. It couldn't have been easy on them. Thank you. Thank you for that perspective."

Like the two truths at bedtime, a true complaint and real love don't cancel each other out, so you can take the true part without giving up your love or defending yourself.

items.title: Catch the Hook: the being, not doing line
items.where: Catch the Hook Before the Story Takes Over, P2
items.my_version: When you catch it, look around and just take a moment to enjoy some free honesty: "Oh! I'm hooked again! That's awesome I could notice it!" Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

Take a breath or three before you finish whatever you were doing. Sometimes human beings need to be being, not always doing. 🙃 Maybe then you'll find there's enough adult around to be nice to your little boo for a second. Or enough Protector to stop something you'd regret later.

items.title: Close the Session: the last line
items.where: Close the Session and Return to Life, P2
items.my_version: And what's next for you two? Maybe it's making food, or just going to bed. Whatever it is, tell your little one, "That's enough for today. We're going back to the life we're building." Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you're still feeling can come along.

Nothing has to be resolved first, and whatever you're still feeling can come along. Going back to your life is part of the healing, too.

items.title: Untangling the Belonging Bargains: ", which is ordinary"
items.my_version: Part of building who you are is untangling yourself from whatever pulls you away from your own knowing in return for belonging. A political tribe might expect consistent positions and predictable reactions, while a family or religion that's kind to you might have expectations that just feel like being good. Most groups expect some conformity. Your family might want a particular kind of son or daughter, and your friends might have rules about what you can joke about or get upset about. But if going along means betraying yourself, that's the bargain. It can help to write down the rules your family ran on, including unspoken ones like "Boys don't cry." Then write down the role you got handed, like the stand-in parent, or the one who got blamed for everything (ST-CA has lists of both, in sections 15.2.3 and 15.2.4).

items.title: Let the Child Be Bad at Things: the closing summary
items.where: Let the Child Be Bad at Things, P3
items.my_version: Give a new interest enough tries to get past the humiliation of being a beginner, when you keep telling people, "Sorry, I'm new." Maybe after that you still genuinely dislike it, and then you may quit. You may also discover a part of yourself that never had permission to exist.

Maybe after that you still genuinely dislike it, and then you may quit. You may also discover a part of yourself that never had permission to exist. Either way, that's pl/ork in its most literal form: play becomes part of forming your identity.

items.title: Borrowed Adulthood in Relationship: the blessing line
items.comment:
i'm trying to instill gratitude and also show that not everyone has this blessing in their life... altho i should probably also not assume that someone does. let's add after that, "If it's more distributed, with various people you can count on for small parts, that can be more sustainable, even if it doesn't feel as monumental."
i'm surprised you didn't notice the next sentence after this is redundant. 
cut "Say they're the one who always remembers your appointments."
items.my_version: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt by people, so some of the healing has to happen with people too. Often it's mostly one person carrying a lot of it, maybe the one who drives you to your appointments and says it'll be okay. Maybe you're picturing them right now.
items.before: Reparenting is usually talked about as something you do alone, or with a therapist. But your little one got hurt by people, so some of the healing has to happen with people too. Often it's mostly one person carrying a lot of it, maybe the one who drives you to your appointments and says it'll be okay. Maybe you're picturing them right now. Having someone like that while you're struggling can be an enormous blessing.

items.title: How to Forgive Without Forgetting: the gold-star aside
items.where: How to Forgive Without Forgetting, P1
items.my_version: For many people, healing does get around to some forgiveness eventually, or at least to not being run by the resentment anymore. It can't be put on a schedule. And you don't have to forgive first to get safe, set boundaries, hold someone accountable, get justice or get better. Then again, active resentment narrows what you see, and your little one stays organized around the injury. And if someone pressures you into forgiving early, what you get is an enlightened-looking act, with the wound gone underground.

items.title: Missing Someone: the inbox aside
items.my_version: All of this happens in you, so it doesn't matter whether they get any of it. And if it starts making you more compulsive, or a bit unreal, so you can't get back to your life, make it simpler: "I miss you, and I care." Some of that same care can go to the part of you that's still here.

Some of that same care can go to the part of you that's still here.

items.title: Don't Give the Inner Adult Away: what "keep whatever you feel" means
items.where: Don’t Give the Inner Adult Away, P2
items.my_version: How do you check that? I'd keep what you feel around them in mind, and look at their track record too. Do they respect a no, or keep pushing on it, and what happens when you disagree? If something outside of them backs up what they're telling you, and it all adds up, that's a good sign.

items.title: Remind Yourself: your son
items.my_version: A real-life child of yours, or a calm pet, can also act as a companion that brings out the relationship with your own inner child. My son did that for me, and I think that's very common for parents. But those are also their own beings with their own needs as well. Let them come and go without making them responsible for the session.

items.title: Just Like Me: "here"
items.your_version: This is sort of a gentler version of Tibetan Buddhism's tonglen practice (which I learned from Pema Chödrön), where we imagine taking in the suffering of others, transmuting it in our heart, and sending out love and peace to them.
items.comment:
cut this, idk how this got put in, but it sticks out strangely:  "Some of them make it worse trying to get away from it. Just like you, sometimes. 😅"
also not sure why it was decided to leave out forgiving
items.my_version: If you've tried Pema Chödrön's tonglen, this is a gentler cousin, and normal breathing is fine. Whoever hurt you might come to mind, too. I'd leave out forgiving them and picturing their childhood here.
